# Labels on data

A picture of data, a diagram or a map must say what each of its parts is. The easy way is a code (a color, a number, a symbol) on the picture and a legend at its side that explains the code. This file is about why to avoid that, and what to do in its place.

## A legend costs twice

- **The eye must jump** between the picture and the explanation, and back.
- **The person must hold a code in their head that has nothing to do with the subject.** To the two things that matter (the age group and its share) comes a third that does not (purple). Small swatches of color are also easy to mix up.
- **The result**: the person does not work it out and skips the picture. If they must read it for their work, the design adds a chance of error to a subject that is already hard.
- **A legend far from the picture, in a different sequence than the picture**, is the worst case: the top of the legend says "Yes" and the top of the chart is the "No" part.
- **A legend that carries values of its own** (shares of income, each as a percent range) next to the percent of the chart makes two sets of percent that the person must keep apart.
- Chart tools make a legend by default. Remove it and label the parts.

## Label the thing where it is

- **Write the name on the part, or next to it.** The lines of a chart get their names at their ends; bars get their names at the bars; the rooms of a plan get their names inside them.
- **No numbers on a drawing with a list at its side.** If a control of a device already has its name on it, a number and a list entry with the same name add nothing. Make the drawing large enough to read, and explain only the parts that need it, with what they do.
- **If a name does not fit, use a short leader line** to it. Draw leader lines at an angle that the picture itself does not use, thus they are not taken for a part of it. A few are fine; many leader lines beat the picture.
- **Fit the names by changing the picture, not by adding codes.** A plan is not a survey: make a zone with much text larger and a zone with little text smaller. A name that sits a little outside its small cell with a thin line is better than a number.
- **When there are too many things to label, label the largest ones** and leave the others for the index. Resist the legend to the end.
- **A sign that is known needs no explanation** (a plane at an airport, a fire extinguisher). Use such signs, and a word for the others.
- **Do not improve a plain labelled plan** by adding symbols, colored sectors and a key in the corner. That is not design.

## No labels that show on hover

A label that shows when the pointer is on a part is a legend that also needs a movement of the hand: the person cannot even look to find out what is there. Label the parts in the picture. A hover can add detail to a part that already has its name.

## Arrange the labels as the things

When labels must not go into the picture (a painting, a group photo), put them next to it in the same arrangement as the things: the names of the people in rows, as the people sit. No numbers are needed. The person still has to match the two, but this is a choice made to keep the picture untouched. A plan of a building with three floors at each side of a hall can lay the floors down side by side, thus each shop name stands where the shop is.

## An index is not a legend

- **A legend explains a code. An index helps to find a thing whose name the person knows** and whose place they do not. Labels on the picture do not replace it: a map with 300 names needs a list by the alphabet.
- **The index says where to look with as little code as possible.** A grid reference ("C8") is a code that the person holds while they find a letter, a digit and their crossing. If the thing has a structure that people already use to describe places, use that: for a network with a ring, an arrow in the color of the line that says on which side of the ring the stop is.
- **A list by one plain sequence** (the alphabet) is found faster than a list cut into many categories, where the person must first guess the category.
- **A name is better than a number where a name is possible.** A bus that shows where it goes needs no route table; a number means nothing with no table.

## When a code stays

- **Make it guessable, or easy to remember after one look.** A train at a railway station, a ship at a pier.
- **Few codes.** Do not make a symbol for each rare case. A timetable where each minute has a color, a frame, a flower and one of five small marks cannot be read. Mark the rare cases with one sign and explain them in a short list of exceptions ("Check before you travel: no step-free access at … until September").
- **A color means something.** Use the meanings that people know: red for danger, green and brown for the height of land, shades of blue for the depth of water. Shades of one color that are laid half-transparent over a map cannot be told from the map below.
- **The sequence of the colors follows the sequence of the values**: a row of shades from light to dark for a row of ranges, and not three shades and then a different color for the fourth.
- **The legend, if it stays, stands close to the picture and in the same sequence as the parts in it.**

## "This" in the place of a code

- **Put the text at the thing, and a pointing word is enough.** A record label that says "This side: … The other side: …" needs no "A" and "B". A sentence "this chart shows…" with the chart next to it needs no "see figure 18".
- **No numbered figures, tables and notes.** Lay the page out so that the place of a picture says which text it belongs to. A note stands in the margin next to its paragraph, not at the foot of the page and not at the end. On a web page, a footnote at the bottom is never read.
- **Text next to the part of the picture that it is about** is better than one long text with references: a short paragraph at each part of a building plan. If the text stays whole, mark in it the words that name a color of the picture, in that color.
- This is not treating the reader as a fool. The attention that goes into the search for a match is not spent on the subject. With fewer made-up obstacles, the person can take in harder things.
- **A code hides errors from the author too**: a plan with numbered rooms and a list can have two rooms mixed up for fifty years, because nobody checks each number.

(In a message of an interface, "this" with no thing next to it is a defect; see "Messages" in the skill `canvas-screen-design`. Here the thing is next to the word.)

## Units in a table

The unit goes into the heading, as the common part. In a long table, where the person has to look up at the heading to know what a number is, a short unit (%, €) can repeat at each value. The heading row stays in view on scroll. See "Tables" in the skill `canvas-screen-design`.

## What to draw

- Names on the lines, bars and parts, and no legend.
- A few short leader lines at an angle of their own.
- Labels next to a picture in the arrangement of the things in it.
- An index by the alphabet for many named things, with a plain hint to the place.
- One sign and a short list for the rare exceptions.
